modern_osis:
Amos — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Amos was a herdsman and also worked in agriculture.

The same Holy Spirit guided Isaiah and Daniel in royal courts and Amos among the flocks, giving each person the ability and eloquence necessary for the assigned task.

Amos warned the twelve tribes that the nations around them would be destroyed. Since the Israelites themselves had become devoted to wickedness and idolatry, he rebuked the people severely.

Yet he also spoke of the church's restoration through the Messiah, extending into the latter days.

Original heading

Judgments against the Syrians, Philistines, Tyrians, Edomites, and Ammonites.

God's warning to the surrounding nations

God chose a shepherd and herdsman to rebuke and warn his people.

People to whom God gives abilities for service must not be despised because of their background or occupation.

The prophet announced judgment against the surrounding nations that had oppressed God's people.

The expression concerning three transgressions and four does not specify an exact number. It means many sins: these nations had filled up the measure of their wrongdoing and were ripe for judgment.

God deals with these nations in ways that resemble one another, but each judgment also contains something particular.

In every age people have shown bitter hostility toward the Lord's people.

How dreadful are God's judgments when he calls his enemies to account!
classic_reading:
[Amos.1.1-Amos.1.15]
Amos
Amos was a herdsman, and engaged in agriculture. But the same Divine Spirit influenced Isaiah and Daniel in the court, and Amos in the sheep-folds, giving to each the powers and eloquence needful for them. He assures the twelve tribes of the destruction of the neighbouring nations; and as they at that time gave themselves up to wickedness and idolatry, he reproves the Jewish nation with severity; but describes the restoration of the church by the Messiah, extending to the latter days.
Chapter 1
Judgments against the Syrians, Philistines, Tyrians, Edomites, and Ammonites.
--GOD employed a shepherd, a herdsman, to reprove and warn the people. Those to whom God gives abilities for his services, ought not to be despised for their origin, or their employment. Judgments are denounced against the neighbouring nations, the oppressors of God's people. The number of transgressions does not here mean that exact number, but many: they had filled the measure of their sins, and were ripe for vengeance. The method in dealing with these nations is, in part, the same, yet in each there is something peculiar. In all ages this bitterness has been shown against the Lord's people. When the Lord reckons with his enemies, how tremendous are his judgments!

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJudgments against Moab and Judah.1–8The ingratitude and ruin of Israel.9–16
The sins of Moab and Judah (verses 1–8)

Evil desires in the heart become visible in many forms, but God examines motives as well as conduct.

People who treat others cruelly may expect to receive cruelty in return.

The surrounding nations were condemned for wrongs against human beings. Judah's sin was dishonoring God.

The people despised the Lord's law, and he justly abandoned them to deception.

The idolatry they inherited from their ancestors did not excuse their wrongdoing.

Some of the worst abominations and most grievous oppression have been committed by people claiming to worship the Lord.

Such conduct encourages others to become unbelieving and to turn toward idolatry.

Israel forgets God's gifts and opposes his servants (verses 9–16)

We need frequent reminders of God's former mercies.

Those mercies make our later sins more blameworthy.

Israel had received help for the soul—means of grace that taught the people how to use earthly blessings well.

Those spiritual gifts were more valuable than the earthly blessings themselves.

Faithful ministers are a tremendous blessing, and God is the One who raises them up.

Sinners' own consciences can testify that God did not leave them without opportunities to learn from his grace.

Yet the people did everything possible to draw faithful believers away from him.

Satan and his agents seek to corrupt young people, especially through the promise of amusement, bodily pleasure and drinking companions.

Many promising young professing Christians have been ruined by drunkenness.

The Lord describes these sins, especially those of people professing his name, as a burden to him.

His patience may be exhausted, but his power never is.

People who reject God's word and add stubbornness to their sins will not escape judgment through wealth or strength.

We should humble ourselves before God for ingratitude and unfaithfulness.
classic_reading:
[Amos.2.1-Amos.2.8]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Judgments against Moab and Judah. | (1-8) |
The ingratitude and ruin of Israel. | (9-16) |
Verses 1-8
The evil passions of the heart break out in various forms; but the Lord looks to our motives, as well as our conduct. Those that deal cruelly, shall be cruelly dealt with. Other nations were reckoned with for injuries done to men; Judah is reckoned with for dishonour done to God. Judah despised the law of the Lord; and he justly gave them up to strong delusion; nor was it any excuse for their sin, that they were the lies, the idols, after which their fathers walked. The worst abominations and most grievous oppressions have been committed by some of the professed worshippers of the Lord. Such conduct leads many to unbelief and vile idolatry.
[Amos.2.9-Amos.2.16]
Verses 9-16
We need often to be reminded of the mercies we have received; which add much to the evil of the sins we have committed. They had helps for their souls, which taught them how to make good use of their earthly enjoyments, and were therefore more valuable. Faithful ministers are great blessings to any people; but it is God that raises them up to be so. Sinners' own consciences will witness that he has not been wanting to them in the means of grace. They did what they could to lead believers aside. Satan and his agents are busy to corrupt the minds of young people who look heavenward; they overcome many by drawing them to the love of mirth and pleasure, and into drinking company. Multitudes of young men who bade fair as professors of religion, have erred through strong drink, and have been undone for ever. The Lord complains of sin, especially the sins of his professing people, as a burden to him. And though his long-suffering be tired, his power is not, and so the sinner will find to his cost. When men reject God's word, adding obstinacy to sin, and this becomes the general character of a people, they will be given up to misery, notwithstanding all their boasted power and resources. May we then humble ourselves before the Lord, for all our ingratitude and unfaithfulness.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJudgments against Israel.1–8The like to other nations.9–15
Israel's privileges do not exempt it from judgment (verses 1–8)

The special blessings God has given us cannot protect us from judgment if we use them as permission to sin.

People cannot expect fellowship with God without first seeking peace with him.

Where there is no friendship, there can be no fellowship.

God and humanity cannot walk together unless they are agreed.

We cannot walk with him unless we seek his glory.

External privileges provide no guarantee without particular, sanctifying grace.

The warnings contained in God's word and Providence are certain.

When he sends affliction, he will not remove it until it has fulfilled its purpose.

The evil of sin comes from ourselves; we are responsible for committing it.

But the evil of trouble is under God's government, whatever human or natural agents he uses.

Henry is explicit that here “evil” means calamity, not moral evil or sin.

That should lead us to bear shared suffering patiently and ask what God intends to teach through it.

A warning given to an indifferent world increases its responsibility before the coming judgment.

How astonishing that unbelieving people can disregard both God's terrors and his mercies!

The ruin of unjust power (verses 9–15)

Power used as an instrument of injustice will rightly be brought low.

Property and wealth obtained and kept dishonestly will not remain secure for long.

Some enjoy comfortable lives, but a day of reckoning will come.

Everything in which they took pride or placed their confidence will fail them.

God will examine the wrongdoing done within their own homes: the robbery they stored up and the luxury they enjoyed.

Splendid and pleasant houses provide no defense against divine judgment.

Instead, their loss may make suffering feel even more severe.

Yet God will preserve a remnant chosen by grace, as sheep rescued from the jaws of destruction by the great and good Shepherd.
classic_reading:
[Amos.3.1-Amos.3.8]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
Judgments against Israel. | (1-8) |
The like to other nations. | (9-15) |
Verses 1-8
The distinguishing favours of God to us, if they do not restrain from sin, shall not exempt from punishment. They could not expect communion with God, unless they first sought peace with him. Where there is not friendship, there can be no fellowship. God and man cannot walk together, except they are agreed. Unless we seek his glory, we cannot walk with him. Let us not presume on outward privileges, without special, sanctifying grace. The threatenings of the word and providence of God against the sin of man are certain, and certainly show that the judgments of God are at hand. Nor will God remove the affliction he has sent, till it has done its work. The evil of sin is from ourselves, it is our own doing; but the evil of trouble is from God, and is his doing, whoever are the instruments. This should engage us patiently to bear public troubles, and to study to answer God's meaning in them. The whole of the passage shows that natural evil, or troubles, and not moral evil, or sin, is here meant. The warning given to a careless world will increase its condemnation another day. Oh the amazing stupidity of an unbelieving world, that will not be wrought upon by the terrors of the Lord, and that despise his mercies!
[Amos.3.9-Amos.3.15]
Verses 9-15
That power which is an instrument of unrighteousness, will justly be brought down and broken. What is got and kept wrongfully, will not be kept long. Some are at ease, but there will come a day of visitation, and in that day, all they are proud of, and put confidence in, shall fail them. God will inquire into the sins of which they have been guilty in their houses, the robbery they have stored up, and the luxury in which they lived. The pomp and pleasantness of men's houses, do not fortify against God's judgments, but make sufferings the more grievous and vexatious. Yet a remnant, according to the election of grace, will be secured by our great and good Shepherd, as from the jaws of destruction, in the worst times.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesIsrael is reproved.1–5Their impenitence shown.6–13
Israel is reproved for exploitation and false worship (verses 1–5)

Wealth obtained through extortion is frequently spent on bodily pleasures and fulfilling sinful desires.

What has been acquired through oppression cannot bring lasting satisfaction.

How miserable are people who seek security in religious practices that Scripture does not authorize!

They show themselves ready to believe a lie.

We should carefully examine whether our faith, hope and worship have the support of God's word.

Stubbornness despite repeated warnings (verses 6–13)

People whose hearts are governed by bodily desires wander from one created thing to another seeking satisfaction.

They labor for what never fulfills them.

Yet after repeated disappointments they still refuse to listen to the One who can meet their deepest needs.

The preaching of the gospel is like rain.

Where this rain is missing, everything withers.

People often search diligently for the food their bodies need.

How much better if they showed the same care for their souls and, where the gospel is absent, went to hear it wherever it could be found.

Israel had persisted in disobedience and idolatry.

The Lord was therefore coming against the people as an adversary.

Soon each of us must meet God in judgment.

If he examines us strictly according to our own works, we cannot stand before him.

To prepare to meet him with peace and confidence, we must meet him now through Jesus Christ, the Father's eternal Son, who came to save lost sinners.

Seek him while he may be found.
classic_reading:
[Amos.4.1-Amos.4.5]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Israel is reproved. | (1-5) |
Their impenitence shown. | (6-13) |
Verses 1-5
What is got by extortion is commonly used to provide for the flesh, and to fulfil the lusts thereof. What is got by oppression cannot be enjoyed with satisfaction. How miserable are those whose confidence in unscriptural observances only prove that they believe a lie! Let us see to it that our faith, hope, and worship, are warranted by the Divine word.
[Amos.4.6-Amos.4.13]
Verses 6-13
See the folly of carnal hearts; they wander from one creature to another, seeking for something to satisfy, and labour for that which satisfies not; yet, after all, they will not incline their ear to Him in whom they might find all they can want. Preaching the gospel is as rain, and every thing withers where this rain is wanting. It were well if people were as wise for their souls as they are for their bodies; and, when they have not this rain near, would go and seek it where it is to be had. As the Israelites persisted in rebellion and idolatry, the Lord was coming against them as an adversary. Ere long, we must meet our God in judgment; but we shall not be able to stand before him, if he tries us according to our doings. If we would prepare to meet our God with comfort, at the awful period of his coming, we must now meet him in Christ Jesus, the eternal Son of the Father, who came to save lost sinners. We must seek him while he is to be found.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesIsrael is called to seek the Lord.1–6Earnest exhortations to repentance.7–17Threatenings respecting idolatries.18–27
Seek the Lord and live (verses 1–6)

We must not listen only to words of comfort and peace.

We must also hear and take seriously the words of God that convict and awaken us.

Whether we listen or refuse, the word he has spoken will take effect.

The Lord still offers mercy to human beings.

But many expect salvation through forms of worship they have invented, even though those practices only strengthen their condemnation.

If people refuse to come to Jesus Christ and seek mercy in him, the fire of God's judgment will break out against them.

They may turn the world itself into an idol, only to discover it provides no protection.

Repentance, justice and divine mercy (verses 7–17)

The same almighty power can easily turn the suffering of repentant sinners into prosperity and joy, or turn the wealth of defiant sinners into complete darkness.

People living in evil times often refuse plain, honest correction.

Good and wise people may conclude that speaking openly will be useless.

Those who choose to seek and love what is good can nevertheless help save a country from destruction.

We should plead God's spiritual promises, asking him to create a clean heart and renew a right spirit in us.

He remains ready to show grace to people who genuinely seek him.

Their devotion will then affect every other responsibility.

Israel, however, had already experienced judgments that passed by the people as warnings.

Now the judgments would pass through them in full force.

The terrible day of the Lord (verses 18–27)

Woe to people who eagerly desire the day of the Lord's judgment or wish for war and national upheaval because they imagine they will profit from the destruction.

The promised devastation would be so great that nobody would gain from it.

For unrepentant sinners, the day of the Lord is dark and dreadful.

When God makes a day dark, the whole world cannot make it light.

Those whom one judgment fails to reform will be pursued by another.

Escaping one danger will only place them before another.

An outward appearance of godliness with no inward reality is a double evil.

Israel repeated its ancestors' sins.

True worship requires that the Lord alone be served.

People professing religion often progress very little because they have little or no fellowship with God during their religious duties.

Sin had already brought their hearts into captivity to Satan and idolatry.

God would therefore send them into physical captivity among idol worshipers.
classic_reading:
[Amos.5.1-Amos.5.6]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
Israel is called to seek the Lord. | (1-6) |
Earnest exhortations to repentance. | (7-17) |
Threatenings respecting idolatries. | (18-27) |
Verses 1-6
The convincing, awakening word must be heard and heeded, as well as words of comfort and peace; for whether we hear or forbear, the word of God shall take effect. The Lord still proclaims mercy to men, but they often expect deliverance from such self-invented forms as make their condemnation sure. While they refuse to come to Christ and to seek mercy in and by him, that they may live, the fire of Divine wrath breaks forth upon them. Men may make an idol of the world, but will find it cannot protect.
[Amos.5.7-Amos.5.17]
Verses 7-17
The same almighty power can, for repenting sinners, easily turn affliction and sorrow into prosperity and joy, and as easily turn the prosperity of daring sinners into utter darkness. Evil times will not bear plain dealing; that is, evil men will not. And these men were evil men indeed, when wise and good men thought it in vain even to speak to them. Those who will seek and love that which is good, may help to save the land from ruin. It behoves us to plead God's spiritual promises, to beseech him to create in us a clean heart, and to renew a right spirit within us. The Lord is ever ready to be gracious to the souls that seek him; and then piety and every duty will be attended to. But as for sinful Israel, God's judgments had often passed by them, now they shall pass through them.
[Amos.5.18-Amos.5.27]
Verses 18-27
Woe unto those that desire the day of the Lord's judgments, that wish for times of war and confusion; as some who long for changes, hoping to rise upon the ruins of their country! but this should be so great a desolation, that nobody could gain by it. The day of the Lord will be a dark, dismal, gloomy day to all impenitent sinners. When God makes a day dark, all the world cannot make it light. Those who are not reformed by the judgments of God, will be pursued by them; if they escape one, another stands ready to seize them. A pretence of piety is double iniquity, and so it will be found. The people of Israel copied the crimes of their forefathers. The law of worshipping the Lord our God, is, Him only we must serve. Professors thrive so little, because they have little or no communion with God in their duties. They were led captive by Satan into idolatry, therefore God caused them to go into captivity among idolaters.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe danger of luxury and false security.1–7Punishments of sins.8–14
The danger of luxury and false security (verses 1–7)

People often believe that those who indulge their bodies and seek physical comfort are living well.

But Amos shows the danger hidden in such ease.

Here are the pride, complacency and sensuality for which God would call the people to account.

Careless sinners are in danger everywhere.

But those who feel completely safe in Zion, become indifferent to God's warnings and abuse their sacred privileges, are in the greatest danger.

Many imagine they belong to God while continuing in sin and conforming themselves to the world.

The downfall of other people should warn us not to be self-confident.

Those entirely absorbed by personal pleasures are often indifferent to the suffering of others.

This greatly offends God.

People who build their happiness upon sensual enjoyment will be deprived of the very pleasures they love.

Those who try to push the day of judgment far away will find it approaching them sooner than they expect.

Judgment upon pride and hardened hearts (verses 8–14)

How terrible is the condition of those whose destruction God himself has declared!

He has power to fulfill his purpose, and no creature can overturn it.

Some people's hearts are so hardened that even illness and death within their own families do not move them to speak of God or worship him.

A field that refuses to be cultivated will be abandoned like a barren rock.

When we corrupt God's worship with sin, we should not be surprised if his providential dealings become bitter to us.

Let all people beware of hardening their hearts.

God will bring down those who walk in pride.
classic_reading:
[Amos.6.1-Amos.6.7]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
The danger of luxury and false security. | (1-7) |
Punishments of sins. | (8-14) |
Verses 1-7
Those are looked upon as doing well for themselves, who do well for their bodies; but we are here told what their ease is, and what their woe is. Here is a description of the pride, security, and sensuality, for which God would reckon. Careless sinners are every where in danger; but those at ease in Zion, who are stupid, vainly confident, and abusing their privileges, are in the greatest danger. Yet many fancy themselves the people of God, who are living in sin, and in conformity to the world. But the examples of others' ruin forbid us to be secure. Those who are set upon their pleasures are commonly careless of the troubles of others, but this is great offence to God. Those who placed their happiness in the pleasures of sense, and set their hearts upon them, shall be deprived of those pleasures. Those who try to put the evil day far from them, find it nearest to them.
[Amos.6.8-Amos.6.14]
Verses 8-14
How dreadful, how miserable, is the case of those whose eternal ruin the Lord himself has sworn; for he can execute his purpose, and none can alter it! Those hearts are wretchedly hardened that will not be brought to mention God's name, and to worship him, when the hand of God is gone out against them, when sickness and death are in their families. Those that will not be tilled as fields, shall be abandoned as rocks. When our services of God are soured with sin, his providences will justly be made bitter to us. Men should take warning not to harden their hearts, for those who walk in pride, God will destroy.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesVisions of judgments to come upon Israel.1–9Amaziah threatens Amos.10–17
The visions of judgment upon Israel (verses 1–9)

God shows great patience, but he will not endure a people's stubborn rebellion forever.

Remembering the mercies we once received should make us humble when later blessings disappoint us, just as the produce of an earlier harvest should teach gratitude when the next harvest fails.

The Lord has many ways to humble a sinful nation.

Whatever trouble we experience, our most urgent prayer should be for forgiveness of sin.

Sin can quickly reduce a great nation to helplessness.

What would become of Israel if the hand that should lift the people instead opposed them?

See the power of prayer!

See what a blessing people who pray can be to an entire country.

God is ready and swift to show mercy; he waits to be gracious.

Israel was like a strong wall God himself had built to protect his sanctuary.

But the Lord stood upon that wall with a plumb line.

It had become a wall that leaned and bulged, failing the test of straightness.

God would measure Israel and expose its sin.

There comes a time when people who have often been spared will be spared no longer.

Yet even then God still called Israel his people.

The prophet's repeated prayers and their earlier successful answers should lead us to seek the Savior.

Amaziah threatens Amos (verses 10–17)

Those who accuse their brothers and sisters in faith often portray them as enemies of the king and nation, traitors and disturbers of public peace, even when they are actually among the best friends of both.

People who use religious office for wealth and promotion tend to suppose everyone else is motivated by the same interests.

But servants who have received a commission from God, like Amos, should not fear human opposition.

Had God not strengthened Amos, he could not have set his face like flint.

The Lord frequently chooses the weak and foolish things of this world to shame the strong and wise.

Yet even earnest prayers and devoted service cannot always persuade proud sinners to accept faithful warnings and rebukes.

Everyone who despises or opposes God's word risks ruin unless they repent.
classic_reading:
[Amos.7.1-Amos.7.9]
Chapter 7
Chapter Outline
Visions of judgments to come upon Israel. | (1-9) |
Amaziah threatens Amos. | (10-17) |
Verses 1-9
God bears long, but he will not bear always with a provoking people. The remembrance of the mercies we formerly received, like the produce of the earth of the former growth, should make us submissive to the will of God, when we meet with disappointments in the latter growth. The Lord has many ways of humbling a sinful nation. Whatever trouble we are under, we should be most earnest with God for the forgiveness of sin. Sin will soon make a great people small. What will become of Israel, if the hand that should raise him be stretched out against him? See the power of prayer. See what a blessing praying people are to a land. See how ready, how swift God is to show mercy; how he waits to be gracious. Israel was a wall, a strong wall, which God himself reared as a defence to his sanctuary. The Lord now seems to stand upon this wall. He measures it; it appears to be a bowing, bulging wall. Thus God would bring the people of Israel to the trial, would discover their wickedness; and the time will come, when those who have been spared often, shall be spared no longer. But the Lord still calls Israel his people. The repeated prayer and success of the prophet should lead us to seek the Saviour.
[Amos.7.10-Amos.7.17]
Verses 10-17
It is no new thing for the accusers of the brethren, to misrepresent them as enemies to the king and kingdom, as traitors to their prince, and troublers of the land, when they are the best friends to both. Those who make gain their godliness, and are governed by the hopes of wealth and preferment, are ready to think these the most powerful motives with others also. But those who have a warrant from God, like Amos, ought not to fear the face of man. If God, that sent him, had not strengthened him, he could not thus have set his face as a flint. The Lord often chooses the weak and foolish things of the world to confound the wise and mighty. But no fervent prayers, or self-denying labours, can bring proud sinners to bear faithful reproofs and warnings. And all who oppose or despise the Divine word, must expect fatal effects to their souls, unless they repent.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe near approach of the ruin of Israel.1–3Oppression reproved.4–10A famine of the word of God.11–14
Israel is ripe for judgment (verses 1–3)

Amos saw a basket of summer fruit, picked and ready to eat.

This showed that Israel was ripe for destruction, because the period of God's patience was nearing its end.

Summer fruit cannot be kept fresh through winter.

It must be used quickly.

Yet the people would not acknowledge either God's righteousness or their own wrongdoing when the announced judgments came.

Sinners keep postponing repentance because they mistake God's delay for a promise that he will never judge them.

Oppressors despise worship and exploit the poor (verses 4–10)

The wealthy and powerful were especially guilty of oppression and idolatry.

They resented Sabbaths and new-moon festivals, when ordinary business stopped.

Many people calling themselves Christians behave similarly.

For people whose hearts are wholly worldly, a Sabbath becomes either a day to profane or a tiresome obligation.

Yet how could we use the day better than in fellowship with God?

Even while attending religious duties, these people were mentally busy with trade and markets.

They thought worship wasted valuable business time.

People who would rather sell grain than worship God show little regard for him.

And those who lose reverence for God often soon lose ordinary honesty toward other people.

They cheated their customers.

They exploited neighbors' ignorance and desperate need, especially in trading the food needed by working poor people.

How many forms of greed and fraud make commerce hateful to the Lord!

People whose wealth comes from the misery of the poor will eventually be ruined by their own riches.

To despise the poor is to dishonor their Maker, who created rich and poor alike.

God remembers such injustice.

He will call those who commit it to account.

Desolation will arrive when they least expect it.

All earthly pleasures, possessions and even life itself are uncertain.

In the midst of life, we are near death.

How bitter will be the grief following sinful and sensual pleasures!

A famine of God's word (verses 11–14)

The worst sign of divine displeasure is a famine of hearing the word of God.

Such a famine is especially terrible during distress, when people most need God's word.

Some will think little of its absence.

Others will feel the loss deeply and travel great distances simply to hear a faithful sermon.

They will suffer the loss of mercies other people carelessly threw away.

When God judges a church that has turned from him, its members' plans to invent a path of salvation will accomplish nothing.

Even the most attractive and energetic young people will perish spiritually without the water of life that only Jesus Christ gives.

Let us value the privileges we have, seek to benefit from them and fear losing them through sin.
classic_reading:
[Amos.8.1-Amos.8.3]
Chapter 8
Chapter Outline
The near approach of the ruin of Israel. | (1-3) |
Oppression reproved. | (4-10) |
A famine of the word of God. | (11-14) |
Verses 1-3
Amos saw a basket of summer fruit gathered, and ready to be eaten; which signified, that the people were ripe for destruction, that the year of God's patience was drawing towards a conclusion. Such summer fruits will not keep till winter, but must be used at once. Yet these judgments shall not draw from them any acknowledgement, either of God's righteousness or their own unrighteousness. Sinners put off repentance from day to day, because they think the Lord thus delays his judgments.
[Amos.8.4-Amos.8.10]
Verses 4-10
The rich and powerful of the land were the most guilty of oppression, as well as the foremost in idolatry. They were weary of the restraints of the sabbaths and the new moons, and wished them over, because no common work might be done therein. This is the character of many who are called Christians. The sabbath day and sabbath work are a burden to carnal hearts. It will either be profaned or be accounted a dull day. But can we spend our time better than in communion with God? When employed in religious services, they were thinking of marketings. They were weary of holy duties, because their worldly business stood still the while. Those are strangers to God, and enemies to themselves, who love market days better than sabbath days, who would rather be selling corn than worshipping God. They have no regard to man: those who have lost the savour of piety, will not long keep the sense of common honesty. They cheat those they deal with. They take advantage of their neighbour's ignorance or necessity, in a traffic which nearly concerns the labouring poor. Could we witness the fraud and covetousness, which, in such numerous forms, render trading an abomination to the Lord, we should not wonder to see many dealers backward in the service of God. But he who thus despises the poor, reproaches his Maker; as it regards Him, rich and poor meet together. Riches that are got by the ruin of the poor, will bring ruin on those that get them. God will remember their sin against them. This speaks the case of such unjust, unmerciful men, to be miserable indeed, miserable for ever. There shall be terror and desolation every where. It shall come upon them when they little think of it. Thus uncertain are all our creature-comforts and enjoyments, even life itself; in the midst of life we are in death. What will be the wailing in the bitter day which follows sinful and sensual pleasures!
[Amos.8.11-Amos.8.14]
Verses 11-14
Here was a token of God's highest displeasure. At any time, and most in a time of trouble, a famine of the word of God is the heaviest judgment. To many this is no affliction, yet some will feel it very much, and will travel far to hear a good sermon; they feel the loss of the mercies others foolishly sin away. But when God visits a backsliding church, their own plans and endeavours to find out a way of salvation, will stand them in no stead. And the most amiable and zealous would perish, for want of the water of life, which Christ only can bestow. Let us value our advantages, seek to profit by them, and fear sinning them away.

[Amos.9.1-Amos.9.10]
Chapter 9
Chapter Outline
The ruin of Israel. | (1-10) |
The restoration of the Jews and the gospel blessing. | (11-15) |
Verses 1-10
The prophet, in vision, saw the Lord standing upon the idolatrous altar at Bethel. Wherever sinners flee from God's justice, it will overtake them. Those whom God brings to heaven by his grace, shall never be cast down; but those who seek to climb thither by vain confidence in themselves, will be cast down and filled with shame. That which makes escape impossible and ruin sure, is, that God will set his eyes upon them for evil, not for good. Wretched must those be on whom the Lord looks for evil, and not for good. The Lord would scatter the Jews, and visit them with calamities, as the corn is shaken in a sieve; but he would save some from among them. The astonishing preservation of the Jews as a distinct people, seems here foretold. If professors make themselves like the world, God will level them with the world. The sinners who thus flatter themselves, shall find that their profession will not protect them.
[Amos.9.11-Amos.9.15]
Verses 11-15
Christ died to gather together the children of God that were scattered abroad, here said to be those who were called by his name. The Lord saith this, who doeth this, who can do it, who has determined to do it, the power of whose grace is engaged for doing it. Verses #(13-15) may refer to the early times of Christianity, but will receive a more glorious fulfilment in the events which all the prophets more or less foretold, and may be understood of the happy state when the fulness both of the Jews and the Gentiles come into the church. Let us continue earnest in prayer for the fulfilment of these prophecies, in the peace, purity, and the beauty of the church. God marvellously preserves his elect amidst the most fearful confusions and miseries. When all seems desperate, he wonderfully revives his church, and blesses her with all spiritual blessings in Christ Jesus. And great shall be the glory of that period, in which not one good thing promised shall remain unfulfilled.
